utility.notes: Georgia Power (a Southern Company subsidiary) is Atlanta's well-established dominant electric utility.

value.name: Georgia Power
value.notes: No Community Choice Aggregator was found serving Atlanta's residential solar customers this session; Georgia Power is recorded as both the distribution and default generation utility.

county.notes: The City of Atlanta spans parts of both Fulton and DeKalb Counties; this record covers the City's own permitting authority (which applies citywide regardless of county line) and is recorded under Fulton County as the city's primary county.

permit_authority.value: City of Atlanta Office of Buildings (Department of City Planning)
permit_authority.notes: Georgia has no single statewide permitting agency — each of Georgia's 159 counties and its municipalities administers its own building department under the state's minimum standard codes (adopted IRC/IBC/NEC with Georgia Amendments), making Georgia a genuinely fragmented AHJ landscape compared to several other states researched this session. The City of Atlanta's own Office of Buildings is the permitting authority within city limits.

interconnection_url.notes: Georgia Power does not offer traditional retail-rate net metering. Per the utility's own page, residential rooftop solar customers choose between two PowerClerk-administered programs: 'RNR Instantaneous Netting' (systems up to 250kW AC; excess energy is credited at the utility's annual Solar Avoided Energy Cost Rate per kWh, summed monthly and applied to reduce the bill; a $100 interconnection fee applies) or 'Energy Offset' (no system size limit, but the system is not designed to export to the grid and receives no compensation for excess generation; this is the default enrollment for any customer who does not select RNR). A separate 'Qualifying Facilities' program exists for customers who want to sell all or excess generation to Georgia Power.

required_documents.notes: The City's own Office of Buildings page confirms permits are processed via the Accela Citizen Access (ACA) online portal and references a general Document Library of applications/checklists, but no dedicated solar-specific document checklist was located and confirmed this session.

inspection_steps.notes: Not confirmed from a solar-specific source this session. The City's page does describe a general private-provider inspection report process (reports due within 2 business days of inspection, ICC-certified inspector credentials required) effective 2026-07-01, but this is a general Office of Buildings policy, not solar-specific.

timeline_days.notes: No solar-specific review timeline was confirmed this session. Note: as of 2025-02-01, the City's Express Permit process (for minor projects with a 30-minute in-office turnaround) requires in-person submission only — online submission for express permits was discontinued — but it is not confirmed whether residential solar qualifies for this express workstream.

other_conditions: Effective for permit submissions beginning 2026-01-01 (fully mandatory from 2026-02-01), the City adopted the 2024 IRC/IBC/IMC/IFGC/IPC/ISPSC with Georgia Amendments and the 2023 NEC with Georgia Amendments
Any permit application with potential tree impact requires a completed Arborist Meeting before submission, per an ordinance effective 2025-06-25 — potentially relevant for ground-mounted systems

permit_fees.notes: No solar-specific City of Atlanta permit fee figure was independently confirmed from a primary source this session (a $200-$400 range for typical residential solar valuations was found via search synthesis only, not confirmed against the City's own fee schedule document, so it is not recorded here).

rebates.notes: Per Georgia Power's own page, neither Georgia Power nor the State of Georgia currently offers incentives or rebates for residential solar installations (only the federal 30% investment tax credit applies) — recorded as null/no-program rather than a populated rebate entry, consistent with the 'absent' rather than 'unresearched' distinction.
